ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached figure shows a triangular frame, with six empty circles on it: three circles are located at the three vertices of the triangle, and the other three circles are respectively located on the left side, the right side, and the bottom side. Therefore, each side contains exactly three circles. Reasoning: The six numbers are 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, and their total sum is 75. Let the sum of the numbers in the three vertex circles be C. When adding the common sum S of the three sides, the three non-vertex circles on the sides are each counted once, while the three vertex circles are each counted twice, so 3S = 75 + C. To make S maximum, C must be made maximum, so put the largest three numbers 13, 14, 15 at the three vertices; at this time C = 42. Thus 3S = 75 + 42 = 117, so S = 39. Verification of feasibility: If the vertices are 13, 14, 15, then the numbers needed in the middle of the three sides are respectively 39 - (14 + 15) = 10, 39 - (13 + 15) = 11, and 39 - (13 + 14) = 12, exactly the remaining three numbers. Therefore the maximum possible value is 39.

method.method_draft: First read the diagram as a triangle with six circles: three circles are at the triangle's vertices and three are on the sides between vertices, so each side contains exactly three circles. Let C be the sum of the three vertex-circle numbers. From the text, the six numbers are 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, whose total is 75, and each side has common sum S. Add the three side sums. The three side-middle circles are counted once, while the three vertex circles are counted twice, so 3S = 75 + C. To maximize S, maximize C by putting the largest three numbers, 13, 14, 15, at the vertices. Then 3S = 75 + 42 = 117, so S = 39. Finally verify the diagram can actually realize this: with vertices 13, 14, 15, the needed side-middle numbers are 39-(14+15)=10, 39-(13+15)=11, and 39-(13+14)=12, exactly the remaining numbers.
